question: After a global transfer from Egypt to Saudi Arabia, how many person records exist? How many work relationships? How many payroll relationships?
answer: One person record — the person is held once, globally. Two work relationships: the Egyptian one is terminated (end-dated) and a new one is created under the Saudi legal employer. Two payroll relationships: the Saudi one is created under the Saudi PSU in a different LDG, and because balances never span payroll relationships, year-to-date figures start fresh.

question: What is the difference between a legal entity and a legal employer?
answer: A legal entity is an organization recognized by law that can own assets, sign contracts and be sued. A legal employer is a classification applied to a legal entity that enables it to employ workers. Not every legal entity is a legal employer — one may exist only to hold property — and nobody can be hired into an entity until the classification is switched on.

question: A client asks why an Egyptian element does not appear in the Saudi environment. What is checked first?
answer: The legislative data group. All payroll configuration — elements, balances, formulas — lives inside exactly one LDG, and an element defined in the Egypt LDG does not exist in the Saudi LDG. It has to be built again there.

question: Explain job versus position to someone who has never used an HR system.
answer: A job is what the work is — 'Accountant' — defined once and reused everywhere. A position is one specific seat doing that work: 'Accountant #3, Finance, Alexandria plant', with its own budget and reporting line, which exists whether or not anyone currently sits in it. When the person leaves, the position stays and becomes a vacancy.

question: When is a correction used instead of an update, and what does each do to history?
answer: An update records a real-world change: it creates a new dated record and keeps the old one, so a promotion on 1 July leaves both grades in history. A correction fixes a data-entry mistake: it overwrites the record as if the old value was never true. Using a correction for a real event destroys legitimate history and can trigger wrong retroactive payroll.

question: Walk through the payroll object chain from element to payment.
answer: Element (the definition) → element eligibility (who could receive it) → element entry (who does, and how much) → payroll run (gross-to-net, held against the payroll relationship) → balances (running totals) → prepayments (distribute results to payment methods) → payment process (the bank file) → costing (to the ledger). Each link depends on the one before it.

question: An employee earns EGP 25,000 per month. What is their monthly social-insurance contribution, and why is it not 11% of 25,000?
answer: EGP 1,837.00. Contributions apply to the insurable wage, which is capped at EGP 16,700 in 2026 (floor EGP 2,700). 11% of 16,700 is 1,837; the employer pays 18.75% of the same capped figure, EGP 3,131.25. The cap moves every January.

question: Why can balances not span payroll relationships, and when does that become visible to a client?
answer: Because payroll processing and aggregation happen at the payroll relationship level, which is tied to one payroll statutory unit and one legislation. A different PSU means different statutory rules and a different LDG, so totals cannot carry across. It becomes visible on a global transfer, when year-to-date balances start from zero in the new country.

question: Which of the six absence plan types fits maternity leave, and why not an accrual plan?
answer: A qualification plan. Maternity is not earned day by day — it is triggered by an event and paid at a defined rate over the absence, and it can carry occurrence caps. An accrual plan accumulates a balance over time, which is the wrong shape. The six types are accrual, qualification, no entitlement, compensatory, agreement and donation.

question: A department has ten people, four of them half-time. What is the headcount and what is the FTE?
answer: Headcount 10 — every person counts as one. FTE 8 — six full-timers at 1.0 plus four half-timers at 0.5. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions, so always ask which one the client means.

question: OTBI or BI Publisher for a payslip? For a headcount dashboard? Justify both.
answer: Payslip: BI Publisher — a formatted, per-employee, printable document, produced from a SQL data model and a layout template and delivered by bursting. Headcount dashboard: OTBI — ad-hoc analysis against live data using the Worker Assignment subject area, no layout requirement. Swapping them is wrong in both directions.

question: What does element eligibility do that an element entry does not?
answer: Eligibility defines the population an element can apply to — by payroll, legal employer, grade, job, department. It answers 'who could receive this'. An entry is the actual attachment of the element to one person with values and dates — 'who does, and how much'. Without eligibility, no entry can be created.

question: A client says 'we need an extra field for equipment number'. What are the first three thoughts?
answer: DFF — a descriptive flexfield on the relevant object holds the data without customization. Lookup or value set — should the field be a controlled list rather than free text. Approvals — what the workflow should do when the field changes. That sequence covers most 'can you add a field' requests.

question: What is the difference between what a job role controls and what a security profile controls?
answer: A job role controls function — what a user can do: the screens, tasks and privileges of, say, an HR Specialist. A security profile controls data scope — whose records they can do it to: by legal employer, business unit, department, position or country. A data role combines the two. Same job role, different profiles, different visible populations.

question: Why does Oracle not deliver a maintained Egyptian payroll localization, and why does that matter for a consultant's value on a project?
answer: Oracle maintains localizations for a limited set of markets; Egypt's statutory rules are built by the implementation partner in elements, balances and Fast Formulas. That means someone on the project has to know the Egyptian mechanics — insurable-wage caps, the tax brackets and bracket elimination, the small statutory deductions — and a consultant who knows them is useful from the first workshop.

question: A raise is approved in July with an effective date of 1 May. What happens in the July payroll run?
answer: Retroactive events are raised for May and June, which were already paid at the old rate. Recalculate Payroll for Retroactive Changes runs before the main calculation, works out the arrears for both months and creates retro entries; the July run then pays them and re-states the affected balances, including social insurance and tax for the prior periods.

question: What is a parallel run, and why is it not optional?
answer: Running the new system's payroll alongside the legacy payroll for the same period — typically two or three consecutive months — and reconciling the two line by line, explaining every difference. It is the only reliable proof that the new payroll is correct before the old one is switched off.

question: Name the three parts of the Ulrich model and say which one a consultant works with most day to day.
answer: HR business partners embedded in the business, centers of excellence owning policy in a domain, and shared services doing the transactional work. Day to day, the consultant works most with shared services — in Egypt the Personnel and Payroll team — because their work is what the configuration automates; the CoEs sign off design in their domain.

question: What is the mandatory annual increment in Egypt calculated on, and why does that matter for high earners?
answer: At least 3% of the social-insurance wage — the insurable wage — not total salary. Because the insurable wage is capped (EGP 16,700 in 2026), the increment is effectively capped at 3% of the ceiling for anyone earning above it.

question: Under the current Egyptian brackets, why might a naive progressive tax calculation understate tax for a senior employee?
answer: Because of bracket elimination. Above defined net-income thresholds the lower bands are removed — above EGP 600,000 the 0% band goes, above 700,000 the 10% band too, and so on until above 1.2 million only the 25% and 27.5% bands apply. A calculator that applies every band to everyone gives senior staff lower-band relief they are not entitled to.

question: What is a subject area, and why does choosing the wrong one produce wrong numbers rather than an error?
answer: A pre-built, governed data model in OTBI — pre-joined tables exposed as folders and columns — covering one domain at a fixed grain. Choosing wrong does not fail; it silently reports at the wrong grain: date-effective history multiplies rows and multiple assignments double-count people, so the numbers are plausible and wrong.

question: Name the three OTBI constraints that catch people, and the three workarounds.
answer: Constraints: no joins across subject areas in one analysis; a default row limit (around 65,000) past which results truncate silently; and predefined grain that cannot be changed. Workarounds: a Combined Analysis on a shared key such as person number; BI Publisher with hand-written SQL; or an HCM Extract for large volumes.

question: OTBI or BI Publisher for a payslip? For a headcount dashboard? For a 200,000-row extract? Justify all three.
answer: Payslip: BI Publisher, formatted per-employee output with bursting. Headcount dashboard: OTBI, ad-hoc and live. 200,000 rows: past OTBI's row limit — an HCM Extract, or BI Publisher with its own SQL.

question: What are the two halves of a BI Publisher report, and which one is closest to ordinary SQL work?
answer: A data model and a layout template. The data model is genuinely SQL against the reporting schema — that half is ordinary query work. The template controls layout and is the new part.

question: Explain bursting to someone who has never heard of it.
answer: One report run produces thousands of individual outputs, each delivered separately to the right person — one payroll run becomes one payslip email per employee. Bursting is the splitting and routing step.

question: Write a valid METADATA line for a simple object from memory, then a matching MERGE line.
answer: METADATA|JobFamily|JobFamilyCode|JobFamilyName|EffectiveStartDate|EffectiveEndDate — then — MERGE|JobFamily|SALES|Sales|2000/01/01|4712/12/31. Same discriminator, same attributes in the same order, pipe-delimited, dates as YYYY/MM/DD.

question: Give two reasons an HDL file would be rejected before any data loads.
answer: A METADATA line appearing after the MERGE lines it describes; two METADATA lines for the same component in one file; a MERGE line whose attributes do not match the METADATA order (pipe-count mismatch); a wrongly cased attribute name; a file saved with a UTF-8 byte-order mark.

question: Can a single .dat file contain two METADATA lines? Under what condition?
answer: Yes — a Worker.dat routinely has METADATA lines for Worker, PersonName, WorkRelationship, Assignment and more. The condition is that each METADATA line is for a different component; two for the same component is invalid.

question: What is 4712/12/31 and why does it appear everywhere?
answer: Oracle's conventional 'end of time' date. Every date-effective record has an end date, and an open-ended, current record ends on 4712/12/31 — so it is on almost every current row in a load and in the tables.

question: Explain the difference between a source key and a user key, and say which one to insist on for a migration that must be reconciled.
answer: A source key is SourceSystemOwner plus SourceSystemId — the record's identity in the legacy system. A user key is a natural business key such as JobFamilyCode. For a migration that must be reconciled, insist on source keys: they are what trace every Oracle record back to its legacy origin and let every variance be explained.

question: What does JobFamilyId(SourceSystemId) mean in a METADATA line?
answer: A foreign-object reference: the column points at a job family, identified by its source-system id rather than Oracle's internal id. The bracket names the key type used to resolve the reference. It is how child records attach to parents in a load.

question: Multiple .dat files are in one zip. Are they loaded in parallel or sequentially, and what does that mean for ordering?
answer: Imported in parallel, loaded sequentially. Referenced data must exist before it is referenced: job families before jobs, grades and jobs before assignments, people before work relationships.

question: What are the four logical sections of a Fast Formula?
answer: Inputs (INPUTS ARE), defaults (DEFAULT FOR), logic (assignments and IF/THEN/ELSE), and return (RETURN). Oracle does not strictly enforce the order, but following it avoids errors.

question: Why does Oracle recommend INPUTS statements over database items where possible?
answer: Inputs are passed at runtime and need no database read; database items are fetched from the database. Preferring inputs makes the payroll run faster.

question: What is a formula type, and why does it mean Fast Formula cannot be learned purely from grammar?
answer: The type fixes which inputs, database items and contexts are available to a formula. The same syntax behaves differently depending on where it runs, and a formula written for one context will not run in another — so the language is learned by reading delivered formulas of the type being built.

question: In words, what is the logic for capping an Egyptian insurable wage before applying the 11% employee contribution?
answer: Take the wage as an input. If it is above the ceiling (EGP 16,700 in 2026), use the ceiling. If it is below the floor (EGP 2,700), use the floor. Multiply the result by 0.11 and return it. Cap and floor first, rate last.

question: A client wants a new field for equipment number. What are the first three thoughts?
answer: DFF, lookup (or value set), approvals — where the data lives, whether it should be a controlled list, and what the workflow should do about it.

question: What actually happens when a sandbox is published?
answer: The configuration changes made and tested in isolation become real for every user. It is a controlled, deliberate step — not an autosave — and the moment at which page and flexfield changes go live.

question: There is no direct database connection to a SaaS pod. Name all four ways to get data out, and when each is right.
answer: OTBI for ad-hoc analysis and dashboards; BI Publisher data models for formatted output and complex SQL; HCM Extract for scheduled or large-volume outbound files; REST APIs for real-time integration.

question: Where is the honest boundary between what a strong functional consultant does and what is handed to a technical team?
answer: Expected of a functional consultant: HDL loads, simple Fast Formulas, OTBI analyses and basic BI Publisher. Handed off: Oracle Integration Cloud integrations and complex BI Publisher development.

question: Someone hands you a table and asks for total revenue. What do you establish first?
answer: What one row represents — the grain. If one row is one order, summing the order total is right. If the table has been joined to order lines, each order now appears once per line and the same sum is inflated by the average number of lines per order weighted by order value. Nothing errors; the number just looks plausible and is wrong. I'd confirm the primary key, check row count against distinct key count, and only then sum.

question: Why prefer a surrogate key over a natural one for joining?
answer: Because natural keys change. Email addresses, national IDs and company codes all get reassigned or corrected, and when a key changes every row that referenced it breaks. A surrogate key is a meaningless generated number that never changes, so relationships stay intact. The working rule is join on surrogates, report on naturals — the user still wants to see the email, not the integer.

question: What is wrong with a table whose columns are Jan, Feb, Mar?
answer: The month is encoded in the column header rather than stored as a value, so it's wide rather than long. It's readable for a human scanning across, but pivot tables, Power BI and most charting tools all compute on long data — one row per observation, with a month column and a value column. It has to be unpivoted before you can group or chart by month, and doing that with the tool's unpivot rather than by hand is what makes it repeatable.

question: Why can't you use a SELECT alias in the WHERE clause?
answer: Because of logical processing order. The engine resolves FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, and only then SELECT — so at the point WHERE runs, the alias doesn't exist yet. You either repeat the expression in WHERE or wrap the query in a subquery or CTE. The same alias usually does work in ORDER BY, because ORDER BY runs last.

question: When does a filter belong in HAVING rather than WHERE?
answer: When it's a condition on an aggregate. 'Orders over 100' is a row condition and goes in WHERE. 'Customers whose total is over 1,000' is a condition on a SUM that doesn't exist until GROUP BY has run, so it has to go in HAVING. Putting a plain row filter in HAVING usually works but is slower — you've grouped rows you were always going to throw away.

question: A colleague's NOT IN query returns no rows at all, and there's no error. What do you check?
answer: Whether the list or subquery can return NULL. SQL has three-valued logic, so any comparison with NULL is unknown, and x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is never true for any x — the result set comes back empty and nothing complains. NOT EXISTS doesn't have that behaviour, so I'd rewrite it that way, and it's the safer default habit regardless.

question: What's the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column)?
answer: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column isn't NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts distinct non-null values. They're three different questions, and the gap between the first two is exactly the number of NULLs — which is often the more interesting number.

question: Why does a LEFT JOIN sometimes behave like an INNER JOIN?
answer: Because of a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause. Unmatched rows get NULL in the right-hand columns, NULL = anything is unknown, and WHERE discards them — so you're left with exactly what an inner join would return. The fix is to move that condition into the ON clause, where it decides what counts as a match instead of filtering the result. The exception is an anti-join, where filtering IS NULL in WHERE is the whole point.

question: Revenue in your report is roughly double what finance says. Where do you look first?
answer: A join that changed the grain. If orders were joined to order lines, every order-level value now appears once per line, so SUM(order_total) is weighted by line count. I'd compare the row count before and after each join — if a join changed it and I didn't expect that, stop there. The fix is to aggregate the many side to the grain I want before joining, usually in a CTE, rather than reaching for DISTINCT afterwards.

question: A join returns far fewer rows than you expected. What do you suspect?
answer: The keys, before the logic. Trailing whitespace, one side stored as text and the other as an integer, case sensitivity differing by collation, leading zeros stripped by a spreadsheet upstream. I'd count distinct keys on both sides and eyeball a handful that failed to match. It's nearly always the data rather than the SQL.

question: What does a window function do that GROUP BY cannot?
answer: It computes across a set of rows and returns the answer on every row, instead of collapsing them. That's what makes running totals, rankings, each row's share of its group, and period-on-period change possible while keeping the detail. PARTITION BY is the window equivalent of GROUP BY, except the rows survive.

question: Your running total is wrong on days that have two orders. Why?
answer: The default frame. With an ORDER BY and no frame clause, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE treats every row sharing an ordering value as one unit — so both rows on that date get the total including both, rather than stepping one at a time. Writing ROWS explicitly fixes it. It's a nasty bug because on data with no ties the two are identical, so it survives testing.

question: How do you keep exactly one row per customer — say their most recent order?
answer: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) in a CTE, then filter to row number 1 outside it. You can't filter a window function in WHERE because WHERE runs before SELECT. And the ORDER BY needs a deliberate tiebreaker — otherwise two orders on the same date make the result unstable between runs.

question: You inherit a spreadsheet full of VLOOKUPs. What do you check first?
answer: The fourth argument. Omitted, it defaults to TRUE — approximate match — which assumes the lookup column is sorted ascending and returns the largest value at or below the one asked for; on unsorted data the result is simply unreliable. On unsorted data that gives confidently wrong answers rather than errors, so nobody notices. Anything new I'd write as XLOOKUP, which defaults to exact match, can look left, and references arrays rather than a column number so inserting a column doesn't break it.

question: When is Excel the right answer, and when has it stopped being one?
answer: It's the fastest tool in existence for a question nobody has asked before, on data just handed to you, where the answer is needed in ten minutes and never again. It stops the moment a number matters to more than one person or has to be reproduced next month — because a spreadsheet has no audit trail, no real access control, and no way to tell whether the copy you were emailed is current. At that point it becomes a query against the source and a model somebody can refresh.

question: Why is Power Query the highest-return thing to learn in Excel?
answer: Because it makes the cleaning repeatable and inspectable. It imports, reshapes, unpivots, splits and joins, and it records every step — so next month's file is one click, and a colleague can read what you did. A folder of manually cleaned spreadsheets contains no such record. And it's the same engine in Power BI, so none of the effort is Excel-specific.

question: Why does Power BI want a star schema rather than one flat table?
answer: Because the engine's compression and its filter propagation are both built around it. One fact table of the events you measure, surrounded by dimension tables of the things you slice by, each joined on a single key. It's smaller, faster and far easier to reason about than a flat wide table, and Microsoft's own guidance says so. Given a flat export, splitting the dimensions out of it is the first modelling job.

question: A slicer isn't filtering a visual. Someone suggests turning on bidirectional filtering. What do you say?
answer: That it's the tempting fix and usually the wrong one. Filters are meant to flow from the one side to the many — select a product, the sales rows filter. Making a relationship filter both ways can create ambiguous paths through the model, make results depend on evaluation order, and slow queries down. I'd look first for a missing bridge table or a model that isn't really a star, and reach for bidirectional last, deliberately.

question: How do you decide whether a calculation belongs in Power Query or DAX?
answer: Roche's Maxim: transform as far upstream as possible, and as far downstream as necessary. If the calculation gives the same answer regardless of what the user has selected, it's a transformation — do it in the source or Power Query, where it happens once at refresh and every report benefits. Leave to DAX only what genuinely depends on the filter context. Otherwise nobody can find where a number is defined, and the same fix has to be made four times.

question: When do you write a measure and when a calculated column?
answer: A calculated column is computed row by row at refresh and stored, so it knows the current row and nothing about the report — use it for something you need to slice, group or filter by. A measure is computed at query time in the filter context of each cell, so it knows nothing about rows and everything about what the user selected — use it for anything you aggregate. The default should be a measure; a calculated column holding Quantity times Price on ten million rows costs memory and can't respond to a slicer.

question: A stakeholder says your measure is wrong in the total row. What's usually going on?
answer: The total row is a different filter context, not the sum of the rows above it. The measure is evaluated once per cell under whatever filters that cell sits in, and the total cell has fewer filters — so for anything non-additive, like a ratio or a distinct count, the total legitimately isn't the column sum. It's almost never the measure and almost always the context, and the explanation is usually what the stakeholder actually needs.

question: What does CALCULATE do, and what surprises people about it?
answer: It evaluates an expression in a filter context it has modified — it's the centre of the language. What surprises people is that its filter arguments replace existing filters on the same column rather than adding to them, so filtering to Cairo returns Cairo even in a cell already filtered to Alexandria. KEEPFILTERS makes it intersect instead. The other surprise is context transition: called in a row context, it turns that row into a filter context, which is behind most DAX behaviour that looks like magic.

question: Someone asks you to 'look at our sales'. What happens next?
answer: A short conversation, not three hours of dashboard building. What decision does the answer feed? Over what period, and compared with what — a number with nothing to compare it to isn't information. Which population counts: are churned customers, test accounts and trials in or out? What would count as a surprising answer? Then I repeat it back as one sentence and get agreement. That sentence is the specification, and it's usually the chart title.

question: Why must a bar chart's axis start at zero when a line chart's need not?
answer: Because they encode differently. Bars encode value by length, so truncating the axis at 90 makes a 2% difference look like a doubling — the reader is comparing lengths that no longer mean what they look like. A line encodes change by slope, and forcing a zero baseline often flattens exactly the movement you're showing, so truncation is legitimate there as long as the axis is labelled honestly.

question: What do you do before presenting a number?
answer: Reconcile it against something the business already trusts — last month's close, the finance figure, the count in the source system. If it doesn't match, find out why before the meeting, because someone in the room will ask. Then spot-check individual rows against the source and look at the boundaries: first period, last period, nulls, categories with one row. And say what I'm unsure about — a flagged caveat costs nothing, a number that quietly turns out to be wrong costs trust.

question: A client has five companies on the org chart. How do you work out how many legal entities to create?
answer: By the commercial registers, not the org chart. A legal entity is an organization recognized by law — its own register number and tax card. Groups routinely run acquired companies as one business long after the paperwork says otherwise, and the reverse happens too. Ask for the registration certificates and count those. Then decide separately which of them actually employ people, because only those need the legal employer classification.

question: A legal entity is a legal employer but not a payroll statutory unit. What does Oracle require?
answer: A parent PSU has to be entered on it. Its legal reporting units are then created as tax reporting units under that parent rather than under the entity itself. That is the shape a shared-services group takes: several legal employers, one entity doing the statutory filing for all of them.

question: Why does business unit design decide how much duplicate configuration a client lives with?
answer: Because set-enabled data — jobs, grades, locations, departments — is grouped into reference data sets and those sets are assigned to business units. Data in the Common Set is available everywhere; data in a specific set is only available to the units it is assigned to. Split the units too finely and the same six jobs get built repeatedly; share too broadly and a hiring manager scrolls four hundred entries to find one.

question: Which decisions in the enterprise structure are effectively permanent?
answer: The legislation and currency on a legislative data group, which cannot be altered once payroll data exists inside it; and the legal employer a worker sits in, which changes only by ending one employment and starting another. Business unit design is expensive rather than permanent, because reference data sets attach to it. Departments, divisions, locations and tree structure are cheap — they move with ordinary effective-dated updates.

question: A department-level HR access requirement cannot be delivered no matter how the roles are configured. What is usually missing?
answer: The department tree. Security profiles scope data by tree node, so 'everyone in Manufacturing and below' is a statement about a hierarchy. If the departments exist as a flat list and no tree was ever built and published, there is nothing for the security profile to grip.

question: A client asks you to add a field for 'highest qualification'. Which object does it belong on, and how do you decide?
answer: The person, because it is true of the human regardless of who employs them and does not change when they change job or employer. The test I apply is: does it change when they change employer? Then work relationship. When they change job? Assignment. Does payroll need to accumulate it across the year? Payroll relationship. Otherwise it is a person attribute. Putting it on the assignment would mean re-entering it on every promotion and losing it on a rehire.

question: An employee is showing as active but was not paid in the last run. Where do you look first?
answer: The assignment status. Status controls whether the assignment is active for HR purposes and, separately, whether it is eligible for payroll processing — those are two different things, and a status that is active but payroll-ineligible is a valid combination used for unpaid leave. After that I would check the payroll relationship's last standard process date if the person has been terminated, and then element eligibility.

question: Why does Oracle group assignments under a payroll relationship instead of calculating per assignment?
answer: Because statutory arithmetic is per person per statutory unit, not per job. If someone holds two assignments and each were calculated in isolation, the social-insurance ceiling and the tax brackets would apply twice and the deduction would be wrong. The payroll relationship groups the assignments so the ceiling, the bracket and the annual accumulation apply once to the whole person. It is also why balances stop at the payroll relationship and never span two of them.

question: A worker who left three years ago is being rehired, and the client says their service should count from the original start date. How do you configure that?
answer: With a seniority date, not by back-dating the new work relationship. The person record is reused, a new work relationship and a new payroll relationship are created, and balances start fresh. The seniority date is what carries continuous service across the break, which is what gratuity, leave bands and notice periods read. Back-dating the work relationship would assert the person was employed during a period they were not, which corrupts headcount history and absence accruals.

question: Walk me through a global transfer from Egypt to Saudi Arabia and give the object counts at the end.
answer: Legally it is a new employment, so the Egyptian work relationship is terminated and a new one is created under the Saudi legal employer. A new payroll relationship is created under the Saudi PSU, which sits in a different legislative data group, so none of the Egyptian configuration applies. The person record is untouched. Counts at the end: one person record, two work relationships with the first ended, two payroll relationships with the first ended. Year-to-date balances restart at zero because balances never span payroll relationships, and whether service bridges the move is a policy decision expressed through seniority dates.

question: An HR business partner asks for a flat retention bonus for the sales division. What happens before it is built?
answer: Compensation and benefits sign it off, because it is a pay element and pay policy is theirs. The HRBP's request is input to the design, not approval of it. Building it on the HRBP's word alone is how a design gets reversed in testing — after the build, and usually in front of the people who did approve it.

question: Who would you ask how the insurable wage is really calculated today, and why not simply read the policy?
answer: Shared services — in Egypt, the personnel and payroll team. The law sets the rule and the policy states the intent, but only the people filing every month know how it is actually applied, including the exceptions the insurance office has pushed back on before. Those exceptions are requirements, and they exist in no document.

question: The payroll run completes with no errors and one employee has not been paid at all. Where do you look?
answer: First at whether they are assigned to a payroll: the run skips anyone who is not, silently and without an error. If they are, check eligibility and then the element entry — eligible means could, entry means does. The pattern worth carrying is that the expensive payroll failures are the ones that produce no error message.

question: Everyone in one legal employer is paid twelve times what they should be. What is the first thing to check?
answer: The salary basis. If it is set to monthly while the annual figure was loaded against it, the run pays the annual amount every month. Nothing errors, because the calculation did exactly what the data said. It is also why the first question about salary in any workshop is whether the client's offer letters state an annual or a monthly figure.

question: In a parallel run, legacy and Oracle agree on a line. Does that prove the line is right?
answer: No. It proves the two systems agree, which is what a parallel run is for. It says nothing about whether either matches the client's policy — an allowance both systems pay flat where the policy says a percentage reconciles perfectly and is wrong in both. Where legacy is the one that is wrong, the correct outcome is a difference raised with the client, not a configuration change to match it.

question: A worker resigns after seven years with a Saudi employer on a final wage of SAR 12,000. Talk through the end-of-service award.
answer: Half a month for each of the first five years is 2.5 months, plus one month for each of the next two is 2, so 4.5 months on the last wage — SAR 54,000 before the resignation rule. Resignation between five and ten years pays two thirds, so SAR 36,000. Figures checked in 2026 against Articles 84 and 85; the contract may be more generous than the statutory floor, and it is worth checking before quoting a number.

question: A rehired employee's end-of-service figure looks too low to the client. What has probably happened?
answer: The service clock restarted at the rehire. A rehire creates a new work relationship with a new legal employer start date, and if the client's policy bridges the earlier service that decision has to be carried by a seniority date. The wrong fix is back-dating the new work relationship to the original hire date, which puts the person in the system during a period when they were not employed and corrupts headcount history and accruals.

question: A headcount analysis returns 4,100 for a company of 3,600 people. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
answer: The subject area is at assignment grain, so a row is one dated version of one assignment: promotions add history rows and second jobs add extra rows. Filter to the row effective today and to the primary assignment and the number comes back to the truth. The habit that prevents it is saying what one row means before trusting any total built on it.

question: A client asks which report they should use to load 10,000 employees for go-live. What do you say?
answer: None of them. The four paths — OTBI, BI Publisher, HCM Extract and REST — are ways of getting data out. Bulk data going in is HCM Data Loader. The same conversation often includes a request to connect a SQL client straight to the database, which has no answer either: there is no database connection to a SaaS pod, and SQL that is genuinely needed goes inside a BI Publisher data model.

question: A load passed import and failed at load. What does that tell you before you read the error?
answer: That the file is well-formed and something it refers to is missing or invalid. Import checks the shape — pipe counts, attribute spelling, date format — and stages good lines; load assembles them into objects and checks meaning, so a failure there is usually a parent that has not been loaded yet or a value invalid on that date. It is nearly always a load-order problem: load the parent, then reload the failures.

question: Why keep the legacy employee id on the record after go-live?
answer: Because it is what makes reconciliation possible. SourceSystemOwner plus SourceSystemId is stored with the record, so any later load, correction or count can find the same row again and a reload updates rather than duplicates. Matching on names instead breaks the first time two employees share one — which in a population of a thousand is immediately.

question: A Fast Formula compiles, runs without error, and pays the wrong amount. Give three ways that happens.
answer: Applying the rate before capping the wage, so the clamp never does its job. Returning the wrong variable, so a calculated allowance is thrown away and something plausible is paid instead. And hard-coding a statutory limit that changes every January, which under-deducts quietly until a statutory return is reconciled. None of the three announce themselves; a QuickPay against a real person, with the expected figure worked out by hand first, is what catches them.

question: A formula fails for exactly the employees who have no overtime that month. Why?
answer: There is no DEFAULT FOR line on the input, so when the entry is empty the formula has no value to work with and errors. Inputs that are usually empty need a default, and the fact that it fails for most people most months is what makes this bug so visible in the first live run and so invisible in a test with three prepared employees.

question: During testing a client says, "can you just add a field for each employee's car plate number? It's small." What is it, and what do you do?
answer: A change request. Size is not the test — whether it was agreed is. It gets logged, assessed for impact and accepted by someone with the authority to accept it. The alternative, absorbing it because it is small, is the most common way a project takes on work nobody agreed to and then cannot explain why it is late.

question: In a fit-gap, what is the difference between "work around" and "descope", and who has to agree to each?
answer: A work around keeps the requirement and changes how it is met — corrections through retro instead of editing a finalized payslip, for example — so it costs no build and needs the process owner's agreement, because their team's work changes. Descope drops the requirement, which is a decision someone has to sign. Neither is a quiet decision: an undocumented descope comes back in user acceptance testing as a defect.

question: A client runs payroll in Saudi Arabia and is adding the UAE. What can be reused and what has to be built again?
answer: The chain itself — elements, eligibility, entries, run, balances, prepayments, payment, costing — is the same, and so are the structures. Almost nothing statutory transfers. End-of-service is 21 days of basic wage per year for the first five years and 30 after, capped at two years' pay and payable from one year of service, against the Saudi award on last wage with a resignation scale. The wage-protection file is a UAE Salary Information File through MOHRE, not Mudad. Pension covers nationals through GPSSA, not GOSI. Each country is its own legislative data group, so the elements and formulas are rebuilt regardless.

question: An HR manager in Dubai asks you to configure unlimited contracts. What do you say?
answer: That the unlimited contract no longer exists in the private sector: Federal Decree-Law 33/2021 made every contract fixed-term and renewable. Then ask when their contracts were last reissued, because the vocabulary usually means the paperwork predates the law rather than that they want something unusual. Practically it means contract end dates are live data — expiry alerting and renewal are part of the build, not an afterthought.

question: Name the three exit routes and say what differs downstream in each.
answer: Resignation, employer-initiated termination, and expiry of a fixed-term contract. All three end-date the work relationship and leave the person record intact. They differ in money and in notice: resignation carries no severance but does pay out accrued leave, and in the Gulf it can reduce the end-of-service award; termination carries severance exposure and the strongest documentation requirement; expiry needs neither party to act, which is why it is the one that catches a payroll team out when nobody noticed the date. All three feed a final settlement.

question: What is a final settlement made of, and which Oracle objects produce each part?
answer: Final pay to the termination date from the payroll run; accrued but untaken leave from the absence plan's balance, converted by a rate definition; the end-of-service award or gratuity where the country has one, usually from a dedicated element; minus any outstanding loan or advance, which is an element entry with a remaining balance. It is run as a QuickPay rather than waiting for the cycle, and the payroll relationship's last standard process date and final close date decide whether a late correction can still be paid at all.

question: The sources disagree about the notice period. How do you configure it?
answer: As a parameter, not a constant — and then get the client's legal position in writing. Where summaries of a statute genuinely conflict, the consultant's job is to make the number configurable, record which reading was used and who approved it, and flag it for re-verification when the executive regulations land. Hard-coding either reading hides a decision that was never actually made.

question: Walk through the Egyptian annual-leave ladder and its two boundary cases.
answer: Fifteen days in the first year, pro-rated once six months of service are complete; twenty-one from the second year; thirty for workers with ten years of service or aged over fifty; forty-five for persons with disabilities; plus seven days for hazardous, arduous or remote work. The boundary cases are the test cases: the person who crosses ten years mid-year and the person who turns fifty mid-year both change band part-way through an accrual term, and the plan has to say whether the new rate applies from that date or from the next term. Figures are Law 14/2025, checked in 2026 — re-verify before configuring.

question: Why is sick leave a qualification plan rather than an accrual plan?
answer: Because nothing accumulates. The entitlement is not earned month by month and carried forward; it is triggered by an event and paid at percentages of the insurable wage that step down over the duration of the absence, within a yearly cap. An accrual plan would model a balance that does not exist. The same reasoning puts maternity in a qualification plan with an occurrence cap rather than a balance.

question: Why can casual leave not simply be added to the annual entitlement?
answer: Because it is drawn from it, not added to it. Casual leave is a short-notice entitlement taken out of the annual balance with a cap on how many days a year may be used that way, so modelling it as its own accrual double-counts the entitlement and overstates the leave liability. It is configured as an absence type against the annual plan with its own rules, not as a second plan.

question: A client wants to stop using positions and manage everything with jobs. What do you ask?
answer: Whether they budget and approve headcount by seat, and whether they need to know that a seat exists while it is empty. Positions carry that; jobs do not. If approvals, budgeting or org charts depend on vacancies being visible, positions earn their cost; if the client simply wants to know what work people do, jobs are lighter and position synchronization is one less thing to maintain. The wrong answer is to decide on tidiness.

question: What is a grade ladder for, and when does a client actually need grade rates?
answer: A grade ladder orders grades into a progression, and grade rates attach pay ranges or step values to them. A client needs rates when pay is governed by the grade — minimum and maximum by band, or fixed steps — rather than negotiated per person, which is common in the public sector and in large Gulf groups. Where pay is individual, the ladder alone is enough, and building rates nobody maintains produces ranges that are wrong within a year.

question: What is the difference between an absence type and an absence plan?
answer: The type is what the worker selects — Annual Leave, Sick Leave — and the plan is the rules engine behind it: who is eligible, how entitlement is earned or granted, how it is paid. One plan can serve several types, and a type must be associated with at least one plan or it does nothing. When a client describes a new kind of leave, the real question is whether it needs new rules or only a new name on existing ones.

question: How would you handle carryover that the client has never written down?
answer: Pin it before building, because it is the rule that creates liability. Ask how many days may carry into the next term, when carried days expire, and whether unused leave is paid out instead. Those three answers are the carryover, expiry and encashment rules, and a client who has not agreed them internally will discover the disagreement in the first year-end — which is a bad time to find out the balance everyone was looking at was wrong.

question: A line manager can open the page but sees no employees. Where do you look?
answer: At the data side, not the function side. They have the function privilege, which is why the page opens; what they lack is scope. For a line manager that usually means the manager hierarchy is not built or their reports are not attached to them; for an HR specialist it means the security profile on their data role does not cover that population. Answering a visibility question by changing a job role is the classic wrong move.

question: Why not simply build a custom role for each department's HR representative?
answer: Because it multiplies maintenance for something an area of responsibility already does. An AOR assigns responsibility for a defined population and drives both access and routing, so one role plus AORs covers what would otherwise be a role per department — each needing its own security profile, its own testing and its own upkeep every time the structure changes. Reach for a custom data role when the scope cannot be expressed as a responsibility, not as the default.

question: A client's offer letters quote basic plus housing plus transport. Why does that matter beyond presentation?
answer: Because the statutory bases are computed from particular components. The contributable wage for Saudi GOSI and the UAE gratuity base are both drawn from the split, so how salary components are designed decides what the client owes, not just how the payslip reads. It is also far harder to restructure components after go-live than before, which makes it a first-workshop question rather than a detail.

question: Payroll ran, prepayments ran, and then a wrong element entry is found. What order do you unwind it in?
answer: Backwards. Prepayments lock the run's results, so the prepayments are rolled back first and only then the run; trying it the other way produces an error that reads like a defect and is not. Then fix the entry, and use mark for retry and retry so only the affected records are reprocessed rather than the whole population.

question: How do hours get into payroll, and what does an overtime element need?
answer: Hours arrive from a time card in Oracle Time and Labor, from an interface with an attendance or shift system, or from a bulk load — and which one is a design decision with an owner. An overtime element needs a rate source, which is a rate definition, and a multiplier, which is statutory: Egypt's Law 14/2025 sets at least 35% above the hourly wage by day and 70% at night, and Saudi Article 107 sets 150%. Sources disagree on whether the Saudi base is basic or total wage, so that goes in writing from the client's counsel before anything is built.

question: How would you configure approvals for a promotion, and what would you check first?
answer: In Manage Approval Transactions for HCM, on the promotion transaction, with an approver type that the client's data can actually resolve — supervisory hierarchy where managers are maintained, job level where they are not, representative where HR owns it. Check that first: routing up a position hierarchy at a client who manages by job leaves the transaction waiting with no path and no error. Then add the conditions that matter, usually an extra level above a salary threshold, and test with real approver accounts rather than your own.

question: A manager says their change never happened. Where do you look, and what are you expecting to find?
answer: The Transaction Console. Most of the time the change exists and is sitting in an approval that never reached anybody — a vacant approver position, a terminated approver, or a hierarchy gap. The console shows where it is waiting and lets a privileged user withdraw it or push it through, which is why that access is agreed with a named group before go-live rather than handed out during the first incident.

question: Your headcount report returns more people than the company employs. What is the first thing you check?
answer: Whether every date-effective table in the query carries its own as-of filter. An HR source keeps one row per version, so a person promoted twice returns three rows, and two name versions joined to three assignment versions return six. After that, check the primary assignment flag: somebody with two concurrent assignments is one human with two currently valid rows, and no date predicate collapses that.

question: Why is an attrition trend built from current rows wrong, even when the leaver dates are right?
answer: Because it restates history with today's attributes. Grouping today's rows by hire and termination date reports each person's current department and grade as though they had always applied, so a reorganization last month appears to have happened years ago, and anyone whose record was later corrected quietly moves. The honest version evaluates the as-of predicate once per period and stores the answer — one row per person per month — so the trend reconciles with what HR reported at the time.

question: An HR specialist can open the person search and it returns nobody. Walk me through what you check.
answer: Separate function from data first: the page opened, so the role is fine and this is scope. Then four things in order — does the user actually hold the data role or AOR you think they do, not just the job role; does its security profile cover that population, remembering a department-scoped profile misses anyone whose department just changed; is the underlying hierarchy true, because a line manager sees nothing when the manager relationship is missing; and has LDAP synchronization run since the change. Nine times out of ten it is one of those, and none of them needs a technical colleague.

question: A client wants a custom role based on a delivered one. How do you do it, and what must you not do?
answer: Copy it in the Security Console and edit the copy. Delivered roles must not be edited: Oracle owns them and a quarterly update overwrites the change, so the customisation disappears without anyone connecting the two events. While there, the role hierarchy view answers why a user can do something, and the simulation view confirms the result against a named user before you tell the client it is done.

question: How does a role actually get to a new hire?
answer: Through a role provisioning rule, in the normal case: a condition on the record — legal employer, business unit, job, worker type — grants the role when the record is created and removes it when the condition stops being true. Manual provisioning exists for exceptions and becomes a problem as a habit, because manually assigned roles are invisible to the rules and survive transfers. After changing a rule, run Autoprovision Roles for All Users rather than waiting for each person's next transaction.

question: An interviewer asks which Oracle HCM modules you have worked with. How do you answer?
answer: Name the ones you have configured — core HR, absence, payroll — and then show you know where they touch the rest: that Recruiting's accepted offer creates the work relationship, that Benefits enrolments become element entries payroll deducts, that Compensation writes the salary record payroll reads, and that succession depends on positions. Claiming module experience from vocabulary is the one thing that ends the conversation, because the second question settles it.

question: What does core HR owe Recruiting, and what does Recruiting write back?
answer: Core HR owes it the structures to choose from — legal employers, business units, jobs, grades, departments, locations — so a requisition can only be raised against things that exist. Recruiting writes back the person and the first version of nearly every attribute on them, at the moment an accepted offer becomes a pending worker or an employee. That is why data quality in a requisition is data quality in your employment record, and why the national identifier belongs in the recruiting process in Egypt rather than in a chase afterwards.

question: What is a conference room pilot for, and what makes one useful rather than theatre?
answer: It shows the configured system to the client with their own data and their own scenarios, because nobody can validate a design from a document. What makes it useful is that the data is real: a payslip for someone they recognise, a leave request against their own policy. Demonstrating with fabricated data produces nodding in the room and a flood of changes in user acceptance testing, which is the expensive place to discover that the design was never understood.

question: What belongs in a RAID log, and why does it matter to a functional consultant?
answer: Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies — the things that are not work items but will decide whether the work lands. It matters because a consultant's unspoken assumptions are usually the project's real risk: that the client will supply clean national identifiers, that Finance will finish the cost centres before payroll testing, that legal will confirm the notice period. Written down, those become somebody's action with a date. Unwritten, they become the reason a go-live slips.

question: A salary correction was entered as an update and it should have been a correction. What actually went wrong, and what do you do?
answer: An update creates a new dated record and keeps the old one, so the system now believes the wrong salary was genuinely true for that period — and anything that reads history, including retroactive payroll, will act on it. A correction overwrites, as though the wrong value was never true. The fix is to correct the erroneous record rather than add another update on top, and then check whether a payroll run already picked up the bad period, because the retro process may need to re-state it.

question: A Saudi client asks why their GOSI file and their payroll disagree on basic salary.
answer: Because the same figure is held in three places that must match: the Qiwa contract, the GOSI registration and the payroll record. When someone updates one — a raise entered in payroll, a contract reissued on Qiwa — and not the others, the filings disagree and the mismatch surfaces as a rejection or an audit finding rather than as a payroll error. The design answer is to decide which system is the source of truth for basic salary and to make the others follow it deliberately.

question: How does the UAE gratuity differ from the Saudi award, in a sentence a client would understand?
answer: Four ways. The UAE accrues 21 days of basic wage a year for the first five years and 30 after, where Saudi accrues half a month and then a full month of the last wage. The UAE caps the total at two years of wage; Saudi does not. The UAE pays in full from one year of service; Saudi reduces it on resignation below ten years. And the UAE base is basic wage, so the salary component split decides the liability. An element built for one country is wrong in the other in at least three places.

question: A client lists nursing breaks, the pregnancy hour and the overtime ban as leave types to configure. What do you tell them?
answer: That none of the three is leave. A pregnant employee's day shortens by at least an hour from the sixth month and nursing breaks are two paid half-hours a day for two years after the birth — both are working-time rules, so they belong to the work schedule, not to a balance. The overtime prohibition during pregnancy and for six months after is a validation on the overtime element. Building them as absence types produces balances that mean nothing and reports nobody can use.

question: How is maternity leave paid in Egypt, and why is that question harder than it looks?
answer: Four months, up to three times in service, with no minimum service qualification — that part is settled. How it is funded is not: some professional summaries describe full employer pay, others describe payment at a percentage of the insurable wage through social insurance with the employer topping up or offsetting. The two readings produce different elements and different costs, so the answer comes from the client's counsel and their insurance office, and goes into the configuration workbook with a name against it.

question: A client says retro did not pick up a change. Where do you look first?
answer: The retroactive event group. It is the list of changes the system is watching for, and a change outside it raises no event however retrospective it looks to a human — so the process is working and the configuration is not. The Retroactive Notification report shows what events are waiting. In Egypt that group is statutory configuration rather than a technical detail: insurable-wage limits move every January and decrees land mid-cycle, so the things that must trigger retro have to be in it deliberately.

question: What is the difference between proration and retro?
answer: When the change was entered relative to the payroll run. A raise effective on the 16th and entered before the run is prorated — the period is paid partly at each rate, using a proration event group and a proration formula. The same raise entered after the run has already processed that period is retro: the arrears are calculated and paid in a later run. The design decision inside proration is the divisor — calendar days, working days or a fixed figure — and it changes the money.

question: A manager says the transfer screen asks for too much. What are your options?
answer: Transaction Design Studio, before anything else: it controls which fields and sections appear per transaction and per role, so salary can be hidden from line managers on a transfer and a reason made mandatory on a termination — configuration that survives quarterly updates. If the request is defaulting or validation rather than visibility, that is an autocomplete rule. Neither needs a developer, and both are the answer to a surprising share of user-acceptance feedback.

question: Explain the difference between configuration, extension and customization in a SaaS implementation.
answer: Configuration is setup the product expects — plans, elements, roles, flexfields, design studio rules — and it answers most requests. An extension builds something new within supported tools: a Fast Formula, a BI Publisher report, an integration, each needing design, testing and an owner through quarterly updates. Customization in the on-premise sense of changing delivered code does not exist. The useful sentence in a workshop is that nothing is impossible and everything has an owner, which stops the client hearing no and the project hearing yes to the same request.

question: A Gulf client wants position management. What do you check before agreeing?
answer: Four things: do they budget and approve headcount by seat, do they need a vacancy to be visible while it is empty, do approvals or succession depend on the seat rather than the person, and is there someone who will maintain positions through every reorganization. Three yeses and an owner mean positions. Without the owner, the structure decays within a year and the client is better served by a clean job catalogue — the maintenance, not the concept, is what decides it.

question: What does position synchronization actually do, and what is the trap?
answer: It makes the position the master for attributes on the assignments attached to it — job, department, location, grade, manager, FTE — so changing the position updates everyone in it. The trap is the override setting. Synchronization with no override makes a reorganization instant and a one-off exception impossible; synchronization turned off makes the position decorative and the two structures drift until neither is trusted. The design question is which attributes belong to the seat and which to the person in it.

question: What can a payroll formula return, besides a number?
answer: Formula results, and the element decides what each one is for. A direct result becomes the element's pay value. An indirect result feeds another element, which is how one calculation creates an entry on a second without anyone keying it. A message returns text into the run results, which is the closest thing the language has to a debugger. And a stop entry ends the element entry — which is how a loan recovery stops itself at zero rather than relying on somebody remembering.

question: How do you test a Fast Formula when there is no debugger?
answer: Compile it, which catches the grammar — a misspelt input, a name with a space where the element has an underscore. Then QuickPay one real person whose answer you worked out by hand first, and compare. If the number disagrees and the logic looks right, add a message result that returns an intermediate value and read it in the run results. Then test the edges deliberately: an empty input, a value exactly on a threshold, someone with no entry, and a mid-period change so proration is exercised.

question: Why would you use a pending worker rather than hiring on the start date?
answer: Because the record has to exist before the person does. A pending worker is created ahead of the start date so onboarding can run — accounts, equipment, documents — and converts to an employee on the day. In Egypt it matters more than most implementations allow for: the social-insurance registration and the labour-office file happen around the start date, and a record that exists beforehand is what lets that work be tracked rather than remembered.

question: A client asks to change someone's working days from five to four. Why is that not a small change?
answer: Because it is an FTE change, and FTE is read by more things than people expect: headcount against workload reporting, leave accrual where entitlement is pro-rated, and any pay calculated on a proportion rather than a flat amount. It is a dated assignment change with an action and a reason like any other, and the reason is what lets somebody explain the pattern later. Treated as an administrative tweak, it surfaces two months on as a leave balance nobody can account for.

question: An employee's leave balance is wrong. What do you check, and in what order?
answer: Four things, in order: when they were enrolled in the plan, which accrual runs have happened since, what the carryover event did at the term end, and whether anyone has made a manual adjustment. The balance is the sum of those, so one of them is the answer. Adjusting the balance to the number the employee expected without reading them hides the defect and guarantees it comes back next year — and the first thing to rule out before any of it is the work schedule, because a wrong schedule makes every duration wrong in the same direction.

question: How does an absence become money?
answer: Through an absence element and a rate definition. The element carries the payment into the payroll run — full pay, a reduced percentage for a qualification band, or an unpaid deduction — and the rate definition supplies the base the percentage applies to. That base is where regional designs fail: Egyptian sick leave is paid on the insurable wage rather than on gross, so a plan pointed at the wrong rate pays the right percentage of the wrong number. At exit the balance becomes the leave payout in the final settlement.

question: A recruiter asks which Oracle HCM modules you know. How do you structure the answer?
answer: By offering, then functional area. Fusion HCM is opted into as offerings: Workforce Deployment for the employment record, payroll, time and absence; Workforce Development for performance, goals, career development, succession and talent review; Compensation Management for compensation cycles, incentives and benefits. Recruiting and Learning are their own offerings. I would say I know Workforce Deployment, specifically Global HR, Absence Management and Payroll, and that I can follow a conversation about the others and name where they touch core HR, but have not configured them.

question: A client says 'we want workforce management'. What do you ask?
answer: Which meaning they have in mind. Trainers and HR teams often say workforce management for maintaining worker records — hires, transfers, promotions, terminations — which is Global HR. Oracle also uses Workforce Management as the name of a feature area for time, scheduling and absence. The requirement gets written against a different module depending on the answer, so I would ask before writing anything down.

question: What is the difference between a talent profile and a model profile, and why does a consultant on core HR care?
answer: A talent profile describes a person — competencies, skills, languages, degrees, certifications. A model profile describes a job or position — the targeted and required skills and work requirements. Core HR cares because the model profile hangs off the job and position catalogue: a clean job catalogue makes gap comparisons and best-fit searches meaningful, and a messy one makes every talent module downstream produce noise.

question: Why is career development described as the module that keeps succession honest?
answer: Because talent review and succession both read the talent profile, and career development is what writes to it. A development goal can carry target outcomes such as a competency or certification, and completing the goal writes the outcome back to the profile. Without it, profiles are maintained by hand or not at all, and the first succession meeting reviews people against data a year old.

question: What happens in a talent review meeting, and what is the box chart for?
answer: A business leader's organization is reviewed: reviewers submit ratings before a deadline, and facilitators run the meeting. The box chart plots the population on one rating against another — usually performance against potential, the nine-box — and people are moved between boxes during the meeting, which is the calibration. Depending on the template, succession plans and talent pools can be worked on in the same meeting.

question: Walk through how Oracle decides which cost centre a salary payment is costed to.
answer: Through the cost hierarchy, for that segment alone. The engine starts at the lowest level, the element entry, and works up — person element, person, position, job, location, department, element eligibility, payroll — taking the first level that has a cost-centre value. If the person has an assignment-level override that wins; otherwise a job cost centre beats the department's; if nothing below the payroll has one, the payroll's applies. The other segments are resolved separately, so the account can be assembled from several levels.

question: Finance reports a large balance in the payroll suspense account after the first live run. What do you check?
answer: Which segment was missing or invalid, and which level should have supplied it. The common cause is a structure created in core HR without costing — a new department with no cost centre — so everyone in it is paid correctly and costed to suspense. I fix the costing at the right level for future runs, and correct the results already posted through the transfer and accounting route, reversing the transfer to Subledger Accounting rather than editing setup and hoping.

question: The finance director wants employer social-insurance cost to show up in each department in proportion to salary. How?
answer: Distributed costing. The employer contribution element is given a costing type of distributed and a distribution set made of the salary earnings elements, so its cost is spread across the same accounts and in the same proportions as the salary charged to each department. Setting it as ordinary costed would land it wherever its own hierarchy pointed, usually one account.

question: Why must the costing flexfield be designed with the finance consultant?
answer: Because it mirrors Finance's chart of accounts. Each segment represents a part of the account string, validated by a value set, and the natural account values must match the general ledger's. A structure HR designs alone produces journals the ledger cannot accept, and rebuilding a flexfield after costing results exist is far more expensive than designing it once with the chart of accounts on the table.

question: When does Finance first see the payroll, technically?
answer: After Transfer to Subledger Accounting sends payroll's costing to Subledger Accounting and Create Accounting, run in Final mode, posts the journals to the general ledger. Before that, costing results exist only in payroll. That is also why project labour cost is not available until payroll has been transferred and accounted.

question: What does an offset account do, and what goes wrong without one?
answer: It carries the balancing side of each costing entry, because the ledger is double-entry: an expense debit needs a matching credit. Without one, payroll produces one-sided entries that cannot be posted as a journal, which surfaces as an accounting error at month end rather than in the payroll run.

question: A manager says the Promote button has disappeared. Where do you start?
answer: With the user's roles and data scope, not the transaction. Quick actions are shown by role — My Team actions come from the line manager role — and the data security attached to it decides over whom. A role removed by a provisioning rule, or a manager whose reports fall outside their security profile, explains most missing buttons. Only once the role is right do I look at the transaction's own configuration.

question: Describe one sick-leave absence from the employee, manager and HR seats.
answer: The employee requests it in Me, sees the balance and attaches the medical certificate if the type requires one. The manager approves it in My Team, through the absence approval rules, and sees it on the team calendar. HR or the absence administrator can record it on the employee's behalf, correct the balance with a reason, and runs the accrual processes. Once approved, the paid or unpaid portion reaches the next payroll as an absence element — which is why an approval after the payroll cutoff is paid a period late.

question: A factory client has two thousand workers with no system login. How does that change the self-service design?
answer: It means deciding how those workers reach the system — kiosks, mobile, a team leader or HR acting on their behalf, or a hybrid where office staff self-serve and everyone else goes through HR. The choice changes approvals, because a transaction HR keys may or may not still route to the manager; security, because HR needs those populations in scope; and training. It is a first-workshop decision, not a hypercare one.
